original_value:
This paper explores how core problems in PDE-based geometry processing can be efficiently and reliably solved via grid-free Monte Carlo methods. Modern geometric algorithms often need to solve Poisson-like equations on geometrically intricate domains. Conventional methods most often mesh the domain, which is both challenging and expensive for geometry with fine details or imperfections (holes, self-intersections,
            etc.
            ). In contrast, grid-free Monte Carlo methods avoid mesh generation entirely, and instead just evaluate closest point queries. They hence do not discretize space, time, nor even function spaces, and provide the exact solution (in expectation) even on extremely challenging models. More broadly, they share many benefits with Monte Carlo methods from photorealistic rendering: excellent scaling, trivial parallel implementation, view-dependent evaluation, and the ability to work with any kind of geometry (including implicit or procedural descriptions). We develop a complete "black box" solver that encompasses integration, variance reduction, and visualization, and explore how it can be used for various geometry processing tasks. In particular, we consider several fundamental linear elliptic PDEs with constant coefficients on solid regions of R
            
              n.
            
            Overall we find that Monte Carlo methods significantly broaden the horizons of geometry processing, since they easily handle problems of size and complexity that are essentially hopeless for conventional methods.

result.paraphrase: This paper shows how core PDE-based geometry processing problems can be solved efficiently and robustly with grid-free Monte Carlo methods. Modern geometric algorithms often must solve Poisson-type equations on highly complex domains. Traditional approaches usually mesh the domain, which is difficult and costly for geometry with fine detail or defects such as holes and self-intersections. By contrast, grid-free Monte Carlo methods eliminate mesh generation altogether and rely only on closest-point queries. As a result, they discretize neither space, time, nor function spaces, and they deliver the exact solution in expectation even for very challenging models. More generally, they inherit many advantages of Monte Carlo methods in photorealistic rendering: strong scaling, simple parallel implementation, view-dependent evaluation, and support for any geometry, including implicit or procedural descriptions. We present a complete black-box solver covering integration, variance reduction, and visualization, and investigate its use for a range of geometry processing tasks. In particular, we study several basic linear elliptic PDEs with constant coefficients on solid regions of R n. Overall, we find that Monte Carlo methods greatly expand the scope of geometry processing, because they readily handle problems whose size and complexity are essentially impossible for conventional methods.
